etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Early Modern English pleasur, plesur, alteration (with ending accommodated to -ure) of Middle English plaisir (“pleasure”), from Old French plesir, plaisir (“to please”), infinitive used as a noun, conjugated form of plaisir or plaire, from Latin placeō (“to please, to seem good”), from the Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂-k- (“wide and flat”). Related to Dutch plezier (“pleasure, fun”). More at please.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) A state of being pleased or contented; gratification.

quote.citation: 2012 April 22, Sam Sheringham, “Liverpool 0-1 West Brom”, in BBC Sport:
quote.text: But the only statistic that will concern West Brom will be the scoreline, and their manager Roy Hodgson will take considerable pleasure from a victory over the club he managed for just 191 days.

quote.citation: 2019, Toro y Moi (lyrics and music), “Ordinary Pleasure”, in Outer Peace:
quote.text: Maximize all the pleasure / Even with all this weather / Nothing can make it better / Maximize all the pleasure

definitions.definition: (countable) A person, thing or action that causes enjoyment.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Acts 25:9:
quote.text: Festus, willing to do the Jews a pleasure

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter VIII, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: The humor of my proposition appealed more strongly to Miss Trevor than I had looked for, and from that time forward she became her old self again; […] . Now she had come to look upon the matter in its true proportions, and her anticipation of a possible chance of teaching him a lesson was a pleasure to behold.

quote.citation: 2013 May 17, George Monbiot, “Money just makes the rich suffer”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 188, number 23, page 19:
quote.text: In order to grant the rich these pleasures, the social contract is reconfigured. The welfare state is dismantled. […]

definitions.definition: (formal, uncountable) The will or desire of someone or some agency in power.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: Use your pleasure; if your love do not persuade you to come, let not my letter.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Isaiah 48:14:
quote.text: He will do his pleasure on Babylon.

to hold an office at pleasure: to hold it indefinitely until it is revoked
at Congress's pleasure: whenever or as long as Congress desires

definitions.definition: pleased to meet you, "It's my pleasure"
(transitive) To give or afford pleasure to.

quote.citation: 1864, Alfred Tennyson, “Aylmer’s Field”, in Enoch Arden, &c., London: Edward Moxon & Co., […], →OCLC, page 55:
quote.text: [H]e / [...] / Had tost his ball and flown his kite, and roll'd / His hoop to pleasure Edith, [...]

definitions.definition: (intransitive, dated) To take pleasure; to seek or pursue pleasure.
